title: Fast and slow: how to tell who is faster in a race

summary.text: Take tiny, quick steps across the room, and your feet fly, yet you arrive late. Speed is how fast something moves: how far it goes in a stretch of time. There are two fair ways to find the faster one in a race. Over the same distance, the one who arrives first is faster. In the same time, the one who goes further is faster. Your child races across the room in different ways, counts claps, and finds that a slow walker with a head start can win a short race but lose a long one.
summary.art: A girl of 7 in a flat's hallway taking tiny quick steps, heel touching toe, while her mother claps beside a chappal that marks the finish line.

intro.hook: Cross the room taking tiny steps, as fast as your feet can go. Then cross it again, walking the way you always walk. Which way got you there first?
intro.text: Fast feet do not always mean a fast walk. In this unit you find out what speed is, and how to tell who really is faster. You learn to count time with steady claps. You find the two fair ways to judge a race. Then you work out why the walker who looks busiest is not always the one who wins.
intro.art: Two footprint trails across a tiled floor: one with many tiny footprints close together, one with fewer, longer-spaced footprints, both ending at the same chappal.

outcomes: By the end I can say that speed is how fast something moves, and use the words faster and slower.
By the end I can tell who is faster in two ways: who reaches the same finish line first, or who goes further in the same time.
By the end I can say what makes a race fair: the same start line, the same finish line and the same 'Go!'.
By the end I can show that how fast I walk depends on how long my steps are and how quickly I take them.
By the end I can explain why a slow walker with a head start can win a short race but lose a long one.
By the end I can count time with steady claps or a clock, guess what will happen, test it, and say if my guess was right.

terms.meaning: Speed is how fast something moves. It tells you how far a thing goes in a stretch of time.
terms.example: A cycle on an open road has more speed than a person walking beside it.
terms.art: A girl on a cycle passing a woman walking on a quiet street, with longer speed lines behind the cycle.

terms.meaning: Faster means more speed. Slower means less speed. We say these words when we compare two moving things.
terms.example: A crow flies faster than an ant walks. An ant walks slower than a crow flies.
terms.art: A crow flying high above a line of ants on a window ledge.

terms.meaning: Distance is how far it is from one place to another. You can measure it in steps, tiles or metres.
terms.example: The distance from your bed to the door might be 6 of your big steps.
terms.art: A dotted line from a bed to a door, with 6 footprints along it.

terms.meaning: Time is how long something takes. You can count it in claps, seconds or minutes.
terms.example: Brushing your teeth takes about 2 minutes.
terms.art: A child brushing her teeth next to a wall clock with a second hand.

terms.meaning: A race is a test of who is faster. Everyone moves from a start line to a finish line.
terms.example: At a school sports day, children run a race across the ground.
terms.art: Four children running on a school ground towards a finish ribbon.

terms.meaning: The start line is where a race begins. The finish line is where it ends. Whoever crosses the finish line first wins.
terms.example: At home, a chappal can mark the start line and a cushion the finish line.
terms.art: A chappal on the floor at one end of a hallway and a cushion at the other end.

terms.meaning: A race is fair when everyone starts from the same line, at the same 'Go!', and goes to the same finish line. Then the only thing that decides who wins is speed.
terms.example: If one runner starts closer to the finish, the race is not fair.
terms.art: Two children side by side behind one chalk line, waiting for a woman to say Go.

terms.meaning: A head start is when one racer begins ahead of the others, closer to the finish.
terms.example: A little brother is given a head start of 3 steps in a race against his big sister.
terms.art: A small boy standing three footprints ahead of a girl on a start line.

explanations.context: This card is about the word speed.
explanations.definition: Speed is how far something moves in a stretch of time.
explanations.description: A thing with more speed goes further in the same time. So speed needs two things: a distance and a time. A snail and a cycle can both go 1 metre. The snail takes many minutes. The cycle takes less than a second.
examples: A cheetah running after a deer is faster than any other land animal.
A bullock cart is slower than a bus on the same road.
Rain falls faster than a feather floats down.
explanations.art: A snail and a child's cycle side by side at a start line drawn with chalk, both facing a finish line 1 metre away.

explanations.concept: Two fair ways to find the faster one
explanations.context: This card is about how to judge who is faster.
explanations.definition: Over the same distance, the one who takes less time is faster. In the same time, the one who goes further is faster.
explanations.description: In the Step Race, you walked the same distance three ways. The way that took the fewest claps was the fastest. In the Freeze Race, you moved for the same 4 claps three ways. The way that took you furthest was the fastest.
examples: In a 100 metre race, everyone runs the same distance. The one with the shortest time wins.
Two ants walk for 10 claps. The ant who got further is faster.
A school sports day race is judged by who reaches the finish ribbon first.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: on the left, two children crossing the same finish line one after the other; on the right, two children frozen after 4 claps, one further from the start line.

explanations.concept: How fast you walk: step length and how often you step
explanations.context: This card explains the Step Race, where you crossed the room with tiny steps, giant steps and your ordinary walk.
explanations.definition: How fast you walk depends on two things: how far each step goes, and how many steps you take in a clap.
explanations.description: Tiny steps come very quickly, but each one goes only a foot's length. Giant steps go a long way, but each one takes a long time. Your ordinary walk has a good length and a good pace, so it usually wins. Runners go faster with longer steps, quicker steps, or both. The same is true for every animal that walks or runs, including humans.
examples: An ant moves their six legs very fast, but each step is tiny, so you can easily walk faster than an ant.
A mosquito beats her wings hundreds of times every second, yet she flies slowly enough for you to run away from her.
A paddler in a boat race pulls long strokes in time with the others. Short, splashy strokes push the boat a shorter way.
explanations.art: Two footprint trails of the same length: one with 16 tiny footprints and one with 6 ordinary footprints, with a clap count written beside each.

explanations.concept: A head start, and how long the race is
explanations.context: This card explains the Head-Start Race, where a slow walker began ahead of a faster walker.
explanations.definition: A faster racer gains a little on a slower racer every moment. In a short race, a head start can be enough to win. In a long race, the faster racer has time to catch up and pass.
explanations.description: In the Head-Start Race, the grown-up took one slow step for each clap. You walked in your ordinary way from further back. In the short race, the grown-up reached the finish first. In the long race, you caught up and passed. Nobody's speed changed. Only the length of the race changed.
examples: In the old story of the hare and the tortoise, the tortoise wins only because the hare stops and sleeps.
A little sister given a head start may win a race to the door, but not a race round the building.
In a relay race, a team with a slow runner can still win if the others make up the gap.
explanations.art: A hallway seen from above, with a slow walker ahead and a child behind, a near finish line marked by a slipper and a far one marked by a cushion.

explanations.concept: Every speed is measured compared with something
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle: is anything ever really still?
explanations.definition: When we say how fast something moves, we mean how fast compared with something else, usually the ground.
explanations.description: You sit on a train, and your sister sits beside you. Compared with you, she is not moving. Compared with the platform, she moves as fast as the train. Both are true. Even when you sit still on the floor, the Earth carries you round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second.
examples: A passenger walking down a moving bus is slow compared with the bus, and fast compared with the road.
A crow sitting on a wire is still compared with the wire, but the wire, the crow and the whole city are going round the Sun.
Two cars driving side by side at the same speed look still to each other.
explanations.art: A girl sitting in a train looking at her sister beside her, while outside the window a platform rushes past.

explanations.context: This card is about who decides how fast a living being moves.
explanations.description: A crow flies slowly while looking for food and fast when a cat comes near. An ant walks faster on a warm floor than on a cold one. A sprouting seed grows its root faster in damp soil. Living beings sense what is around them and change how fast they move. Scientists argue about how much of this is choice.
examples: You walk slowly in a temple and fast when you are late for the school bus.
A cat creeps slowly towards a pigeon, then springs at top speed.
A moong sprout's root grows downwards fastest where the cotton is wet.

perspectives.who: Many biologists who study plant and animal behaviour
perspectives.explanation: Living beings sense and decide. A crow, an ant and a sprouting seed each change their speed to suit what they sense, and that is a choice.
For an ant or a plant, speed changes are automatic responses. Warmth makes their body chemistry run faster, the way warm honey runs faster than cold honey.

explanations.art: A crow gliding slowly over a rooftop, and the same crow speeding away from a cat on a wall.

agreed.text: Speed is how far something goes in a stretch of time.
agreed.evidence: Every speed we measure, from a runner on a track to a train, is worked out from a distance and a time.

agreed.text: To compare two speeds fairly, keep either the distance or the time the same.
agreed.evidence: Races at school and at the Olympics are run over the same distance, from the same start, at the same signal.

agreed.text: How fast a person or another animal walks or runs depends on how long their steps are and how often they take them.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who film runners measure both the length of each stride and the number of strides each second.

agreed.text: Light is the fastest thing there is. In empty space it travels about 3 lakh kilometres every second.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the speed of light in many ways since the 1600s, and every careful measurement agrees.

challenging.claim: The one whose legs move fastest is always the fastest.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A fast runner's legs do move quickly.
challenging.against: In the Step Race, tiny quick steps lost to ordinary walking. Each tiny step went only a short way. Speed depends on step length as well as how quick the steps are.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: judging speed by how busy the legs look.

challenging.claim: Slow and steady always wins the race.
challenging.who: Many people, after the story of the hare and the tortoise
challenging.for: A racer who never stops can beat a faster racer who stops for a long rest.
challenging.against: If the faster racer does not stop, the faster racer wins. In the story, the tortoise wins because the hare sleeps, not because slow is better.
challenging.context: This card is about what the hare and tortoise story really shows.

challenging.claim: A race is fair as long as everyone runs as hard as they can.
challenging.who: Some children playing races at home
challenging.against: If one runner starts closer to the finish, or goes before 'Go!', the race is not fair. A fair race needs the same start, the same finish and the same signal.
challenging.context: This card is about what makes a race fair.

challenging.claim: Nothing can travel faster than light.
challenging.who: Physicists, following Albert Einstein's work from 1905
challenging.for: In over a hundred years of tests, nothing carrying matter or a message has been measured going faster than light in empty space.
challenging.against: Nobody has found anything faster. Scientists still keep testing the limit, because they do not yet know why it exists.
challenging.context: This card is about the fastest speed there is.

big_questions.q: You are sitting still. But the Earth carries you round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. So are you still or moving?
big_questions.hint: Still compared with what? Moving compared with what? Can both answers be true?

big_questions.q: A snail is slow compared with you. Compared with a sprouting seed's root, is the snail slow or fast?
big_questions.hint: Is 'slow' something a snail has, or something we say when we compare?

big_questions.q: Your tiny steps came fast, but you arrived late. When something looks busy, is it always getting somewhere?
big_questions.hint: Think of the ant's legs and the mosquito's wings. What else counts besides how quick each movement is?

big_questions.q: A plant grows slower than you can see. Does a plant feel time passing the way you do?
big_questions.hint: A plant's day is full of slow growing and turning towards light. What would a day feel like if you lived at a plant's speed?

big_questions.q: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us. So when you look at the Sun, are you seeing it as it is now?
big_questions.hint: Never look straight at the Sun. Just think: if the light is 8 minutes old, what are you really seeing?

story.title: The Boat That Splashed the Most
story.note: A made-up story. Anju, Joel and Shiny Chechi are made up. Chechi means elder sister in Malayalam, and people use it for aunts and older cousins too. The Nehru Trophy Boat Race really is held on Punnamada Lake in Alappuzha, Kerala, and rowers really do keep time with boat songs called vanchipattu. Women's teams race in Kerala boat races too.
text: It was the day of the boat race in Alappuzha. The banks of Punnamada Lake were packed with people. Some held umbrellas against the hot sun. Some sat in trees to see better. Anju was seven. She stood at the very front, holding her cousin Joel's hand. Joel was eight, and he had come all the way from Bengaluru to watch.

Anju's aunt, Shiny Chechi, was rowing today. She was in the women's race, in a long green boat with twenty-five other women. Each woman held a short wooden oar. A singer stood in the boat, to sing the boat song.
"Which boat will win?" asked Joel.
"Chechi's boat," said Anju at once.
"You only say that because she is your aunt," said Joel.
Then a whistle blew, and the boats shot forward.
The blue boat was the noisiest. Its rowers dug their oars in very fast. Splash, splash, splash, splash. Water flew up in white sprays. The crowd cheered for the blue boat.
"Look at them go!" shouted Joel. "Their oars are the fastest. Blue will win!"

Anju watched the green boat. Its oars did not look fast at all. All twenty-five oars went into the water at the same moment. Each woman pulled her oar all the way back, long and strong. Then all the oars came up together. The singer sang, and every pull came on the beat of the song.

Anju began to count the green boat's pulls. One, two, three, four. She counted the blue boat's splashes too. The blue boat made almost twice as many splashes. But it was not getting further ahead. It was falling behind.
"Joel," said Anju. "Watch the boats, not the oars."
Joel looked. The green boat was creeping ahead. First by a little. Then by half a boat. Then by a whole boat.
"But the blue oars are faster!" said Joel. "How can they be losing?"

Anju thought about it. She watched one green oar go into the water. It pulled the water a long way back, and the boat slid a long way forward. Then she watched a blue oar. It went in, made a big splash, and came out again almost at once. It hardly pulled any water back at all. And the blue rowers were not pulling together. Some oars went in while others came out.
"Each green pull moves the boat a long way," said Anju slowly. "Each blue pull moves it only a little. So the blue boat needs lots and lots of pulls to go as far as one green pull."
"So fast oars are not enough?" asked Joel.
"No," said Anju. "It is how far each pull goes, and how many pulls you do. You need both."
The green boat crossed the finish line first, a whole boat ahead. The crowd roared. Anju jumped up and down. Joel jumped too, even though he had cheered for blue.
Later, Shiny Chechi came up the bank, wet and laughing. Her arms were tired, she said, but her heart was full.
"Chechi," said Joel, "Anju says your boat won because of long pulls. Is that true?"

"Anju is right," said Shiny Chechi. "A short, quick pull mostly throws water into the air. A long pull pushes water back, and the water pushes the boat forward. And the song matters too. It keeps all twenty-five of us pulling at the same moment. If we pulled at different times, our pulls would not add up."
Joel thought about it all the way home on the bus. At the bus stop, he tried walking with tiny, quick steps. Anju walked beside him with her ordinary steps. She reached the gate first.
"Long pulls," said Joel, laughing. "I know, I know."
story.epiphany: The boat with the fastest oars was not the fastest boat. How far each pull went mattered as much as how many pulls there were.
ask: Why did Joel think the blue boat would win?
What did Anju count, and what did she notice?
Why did the song help the green boat go faster?
Where else might looking busy not mean going fast?

experiments.title: The Step Race: tiny steps, giant steps or my ordinary walk?
experiments.context: In this experiment you walk the same distance three ways: with tiny quick steps (heel touching toe), with giant steps and with your ordinary walk. A grown-up claps to count the time. You find out which way is fastest.
experiments.question: Which gets me across the room fastest: tiny quick steps, giant steps, or my ordinary walk?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which way will take the fewest claps: tiny quick steps, giant steps or your ordinary walk? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Walk the same path every time, from the same start chappal to the same finish chappal. The same person claps every time, at the same steady speed, about one clap each second. Only the kind of step changes. Walk each way three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a clear path about 4 metres long, for example along a hallway or across the main room
2 chappals, to mark the start line and the finish line
a phone stopwatch or a wall clock with a second hand, to help the grown-up clap steadily (not needed if they can count seconds)
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.safety: Walk, never run, indoors. Move chairs and toys off the path. Walk barefoot rather than in socks on smooth tiles, so you do not slip.

schedule.what: Guess, then walk the same path with tiny steps, giant steps and an ordinary walk, three times each, while a grown-up claps.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Circle the way that took the fewest claps. Draw the two footprint trails: tiny steps and ordinary steps.

setup.art: A hallway with one chappal at each end, about 4 metres apart, and a girl standing behind the first chappal.
setup.caption: 1. Put a chappal at the start and one at the finish.

setup.art: A woman clapping while looking at a phone stopwatch, and a girl walking with tiny steps, heel nearly touching toe.
setup.caption: 2. Walk with tiny quick steps while a grown-up claps.

setup.art: The same girl taking long giant steps along the hallway, arms out for balance.
setup.caption: 3. Walk with giant steps.

setup.art: The girl walking normally, and a results table on paper with clap numbers written in.
setup.caption: 4. Walk in your ordinary way, then write the claps in the table.

flow.do: 1. Put one chappal at the start and one about 4 metres away. 2. Draw the results table. 3. Ask your child to guess which way will be fastest, and why.
flow.say: You will walk to the far chappal three ways. Tiny quick steps, giant steps, and your ordinary walk. Which way will take the fewest claps? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which way will be fastest? Tiny steps, giant steps or ordinary walking? Why?

good: Tiny steps, because my feet move fastest.
Giant steps, because I need fewer steps.
Ordinary walking, because that is how I usually walk.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as your child gives a reason. Write the guess in the table before the first try.

flow.do: 1. Practise clapping once each second, looking at the phone stopwatch or the clock. 2. Ask your child to clap with you for 10 claps.
flow.say: My claps are our clock. I will clap once every second, slow and steady. Clap with me. One, two, three.
flow.kid: The claps are our clock. Clap with the grown-up. One clap each second.
flow.parent: A steady clap matters more than an exact one. Keep the same pace for every try, so the race is fair.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands behind the start chappal. 2. Say 'Go!' and start clapping. 3. Your child walks to the finish with tiny steps, heel touching toe each time, as fast as the feet can go. 4. Count claps until they pass the finish chappal. 5. Count their steps too. 6. Do three tries.
flow.say: Tiny steps now. Put your heel right against your toes each time. Make your feet go as fast as you can. Ready? Go!
flow.kid: Take tiny steps, heel touching toe, as fast as your feet can go. Walk, do not run.
flow.parent: Expect many steps and quite a lot of claps. The feet look very busy. Write the claps for each try in the table.

flow.do: 1. Now your child walks with giant steps, as long as they can safely take. 2. Count claps and steps, three tries. 3. Then they walk in their ordinary way, three tries.
flow.say: Now giant steps, as long as you can, but do not jump. Then your ordinary walk. Watch how many steps you need each time.
flow.kid: Now take giant steps. Then walk the way you always walk.
flow.parent: Giant steps need few steps, but each one is slow. The ordinary walk usually takes the fewest claps. If tiny steps win or tie, look at the step counts together and talk about why.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which way won? Which way had the busiest feet? Why did the busy feet not win?
flow.kid: Which way won? Why did the tiny steps not win?

ask.q: Why did the tiny steps take more claps?
good: Each step went only a little way.
I needed lots of steps to get there.
My feet were fast but my steps were short.

ask.q: Why were giant steps not the fastest?
good: Each giant step took a long time.
I had to balance and go slowly.

flow.parent: This is the heart of the unit. Speed depends on how far each step goes and how often a step comes. The ordinary walk mixes a good length with a good pace. Say the word speed: how far you go in a stretch of time.

check.q: Kavya's tiny steps came very fast, but she took more claps to cross the room. Why?
options: Each tiny step went only a short way
check.why: Each tiny step covered only a foot's length. Even many quick steps add up to a short way in each clap.

experiments.title: The Head-Start Race: can a slow walker win?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up walks very slowly but starts ahead of you. You walk in your ordinary way from further back. You find out who wins a short race and who wins a long race.
experiments.question: If a slow walker starts ahead of me, who wins a short race, and who wins a long race?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The grown-up walks very slowly but starts 4 big steps ahead. Who will win the short race? Who will win the long race? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The grown-up walks at the same slow speed every time: one heel-to-toe step for each clap. You walk your ordinary way every time. Both of you start at the same 'Go!'. The head start stays the same. Only the finish line changes.

materials.item: a clear path about 5 metres long, for example from one end of the hall through a doorway
3 chappals or slippers, to mark the two start lines and the near finish line
a cushion, to mark the far finish line
a second cushion or a paper slip, to mark where you catch up

experiments.safety: Walk, never run, indoors. Clear the path, and walk barefoot on smooth tiles.

schedule.what: Guess, then race a slow grown-up with a head start, over a short race and a long race.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the path with both start lines, both finish lines and the place where you caught up.

setup.art: A hallway from above: a child's chappal at the back, a grown-up's chappal 4 big steps ahead, a slipper 2 foot-lengths beyond that, and a cushion 3 big steps further on.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the two starts and the two finish lines.

setup.art: A woman walking heel-to-toe and clapping, while a girl walks behind her from further back.
setup.caption: 2. The grown-up claps and takes one heel-to-toe step each clap.

setup.art: The girl passing the woman halfway along the hallway, with a cushion marking where she caught up.
setup.caption: 3. Mark where you catch up.

flow.do: 1. Put your child's chappal at the back of the path. 2. Take 4 big steps forward and put your own chappal there. 3. Put a slipper 2 of your foot-lengths past your chappal. That is the near finish. 4. Put a cushion 3 big steps past your chappal. That is the far finish.
flow.say: I walk very slowly, one heel-to-toe step for each clap. But I start 4 big steps ahead of you. Who will win the short race to the slipper? Who will win the long race to the cushion? Why?
flow.kid: The grown-up is slow but starts ahead. Who wins the short race? Who wins the long one? Why?

good: You will win the short race, because you are ahead.
I will win the long one, because I am faster.
You will win both, because you start ahead.

flow.parent: Heel-to-toe means the heel of your front foot touches the toes of your back foot. One step each clap keeps your speed the same every time.

flow.do: 1. Short race: both stand at your start lines. 2. Say 'Go!'. 3. You clap and take one heel-to-toe step each clap. 4. Your child walks in their ordinary way. 5. Who passes the slipper first? 6. Do it twice.
flow.say: Short race, to the slipper. Ready? Go! Clap, step. Clap, step. Who got there first?
flow.kid: Walk your ordinary way to the slipper. Who got there first?
flow.parent: The grown-up needs only 2 slow steps, so the grown-up should win. Your child is catching up, but runs out of race.

flow.do: 1. Long race: the same starts, but the finish is the cushion. 2. Say 'Go!' and race again. 3. Watch for the moment your child draws level with you. 4. Put the second cushion or a paper slip there. 5. Do it twice.
flow.say: Long race, to the cushion. Watch the moment you catch up with me. We will mark that place.
flow.kid: Now race to the cushion. Where did you catch up?
flow.parent: Your child should catch up a little after the slipper and win the long race clearly. Nobody's speed changed. Only the length of the race did.

flow.do: Look at the table and the catch-up mark. Ask what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: I won one race and you won the other. Our speeds stayed the same. So what decided who won?
flow.kid: One race each. What decided who won?

ask.q: Why did you win the long race but not the short one?
good: I was catching up all the time, and the long race gave me time to pass.
The short race ended before I caught up.
My head start was smaller, but I was faster.

check.q: A slow walker starts ahead of a fast walker. Where must the finish line be for the fast walker to win?
options: Past the place where the fast walker catches up
Right at the slow walker's start
check.why: The fast walker gains a little every clap. Only after the catch-up place does the fast walker get ahead.

activities.title: The Freeze Race: who goes furthest in 4 claps?
activities.context: In this activity you move for 4 claps in three different ways: crawling, hopping and tiptoeing. When the claps stop, you freeze. The way that took you furthest is the fastest.

materials.item: a clear stretch of floor, about 5 metres
a chappal to mark the start, and 3 paper slips to mark where you freeze

activities.safety: Hop on a mat or a durrie, not on wet or smooth tiles.

schedule.what: Crawl, hop and tiptoe for 4 claps each, and mark where you freeze.

activities.record: Write C, H or T on each paper slip. Draw the three slips on a line, with the furthest one circled.

setup.art: A boy crawling from a chappal on the floor while his mother claps.
setup.caption: 1. Crawl from the chappal for 4 claps, then freeze.

setup.art: A paper slip with the letter C on the floor where the crawler stopped.
setup.caption: 2. Put a paper slip where you froze.

setup.art: Three paper slips, C, H and T, at different distances from the chappal.
setup.caption: 3. Hop, then tiptoe, and compare the three slips.

flow.do: 1. Put the chappal at the start. 2. Ask your child which way will go furthest in 4 claps: crawling, hopping or tiptoeing.
flow.say: You will move for 4 claps, then freeze. Which way will take you furthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Crawl, hop or tiptoe for 4 claps. Which goes furthest? Why?

flow.do: 1. Your child crawls from the chappal while you clap 4 slow claps. 2. Say 'Freeze!' 3. Put a paper slip by their hands. 4. Do the same for hopping on two feet and for tiptoeing.
flow.say: Go! One, two, three, four. Freeze! Put your slip down right there.
flow.kid: Move until four claps. Then freeze. Put your slip down.
flow.parent: Clap at the same steady pace each time, so the time stays the same.

flow.do: Look at the three slips together.
flow.say: Every way had the same 4 claps. Which slip is furthest? That way was the fastest.
flow.kid: Which slip is furthest? That way was the fastest.

ask.q: How do you know which way was fastest?
good: It went furthest in the same claps.
Its slip is furthest from the chappal.

flow.parent: This is one of the two fair ways to judge speed: keep the time the same, and see who goes further.

activities.title: The Clap Clock: can you count seconds?
activities.context: In this activity you learn to count seconds by clapping, and check yourself against a real clock. Steady claps let you time a race without a stopwatch.

materials.item: a phone stopwatch or a wall clock with a second hand

schedule.what: Clap along with a clock, then count 10 seconds with your eyes shut and check.

activities.record: Write how many seconds the clock showed when you thought 10 seconds had passed. Try three times.

setup.art: A girl watching the second hand of a wall clock and clapping each time it ticks.
setup.caption: 1. Clap once each time the second hand ticks.

setup.art: The girl with her eyes shut, counting on her fingers, while her grandmother watches a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Shut your eyes and count 10 claps. A grown-up watches the clock.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the second hand of a clock, or a phone stopwatch. 2. Clap together once each second, for 20 seconds.
flow.say: One second is about as long as it takes to say 'one Kochi'. Clap each time the clock ticks. One Kochi, two Kochi, three Kochi.
flow.kid: Clap each time the clock ticks. Say 'one Kochi, two Kochi'.

flow.do: 1. Start the stopwatch without your child seeing it. 2. Your child shuts their eyes and claps 10 steady claps. 3. Stop the stopwatch at the tenth clap. 4. Do it three times.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Clap 10 times, once for each second, as steady as you can. I will see what the clock says.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Clap 10 steady claps, one for each second.
flow.parent: Most children clap too fast at first, so 10 claps may take only 5 or 6 seconds. Saying 'one Kochi' between claps slows them down.

flow.do: Write down the three results and talk about them.
flow.say: How close did you get to 10 seconds? Why does a clock help in a race?
flow.kid: How close were you? Why does a clock help in a race?

ask.q: Why does it matter that the claps are steady?
good: So every racer gets the same kind of claps.
If the claps speed up, the race is not fair.

activities.title: Faster Than Me? A card sort
activities.context: In this activity you sort cards of living beings and machines into two groups: faster than you running, and slower than you running. Then you turn the cards over to check.

materials.item: 14 small cards cut from old paper, with one name on each (listed in the steps)
two sheets of paper headed FASTER THAN ME and SLOWER THAN ME

schedule.what: Sort 14 cards into faster and slower than you, then check the answers.

activities.record: Write how many cards you sorted right. Draw the one that surprised you most.

setup.art: Fourteen small paper cards on a floor mat, with words like snail, crow, cheetah and bamboo.
setup.caption: 1. Write one name on each card.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper headed FASTER THAN ME and SLOWER THAN ME, with cards on each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the cards onto the two sheets.

flow.do: Write one name on each of the 14 cards. The names are in the note below.
flow.parent: The 14 names: a snail, an ant, a tortoise, a mosquito, a bullock cart, a growing bamboo, the hour hand of a clock, a dog running, a crow flying, a cheetah, a cycle on an open road, a train, a raindrop falling and an aeroplane.
flow.say: Each card is a living being or a machine. Is each one faster or slower than you when you run?
flow.kid: Is each one faster or slower than you running?

flow.do: Your child puts each card on FASTER THAN ME or SLOWER THAN ME.
flow.say: Put each card on a sheet. Tell me why for each one.
flow.kid: Put each card on a sheet. Say why.

flow.do: Check together. Slower than a running child: snail, ant, tortoise, mosquito, bullock cart, bamboo, the hour hand. Faster: the dog, crow, cheetah, cycle, train, raindrop and aeroplane.
flow.say: The mosquito beats her wings hundreds of times each second. Yet you can run away from her. Why?
flow.kid: A mosquito's wings are very fast. Why is she slow?

ask.q: Why is the mosquito slow, even with such fast wings?
good: Each wing beat moves her only a tiny way.
Busy wings are not the same as speed.

flow.parent: Some bamboo can grow almost a metre in one day, the fastest growth of any plant. That is still far slower than a snail crawls, but very fast for a plant.

activities.title: The Slow Race: who can be last without stopping?
activities.context: In this activity the slowest walker wins. You must keep moving all the time and never stand still. Many Indian schools have a slow cycle race on sports day, where the last cyclist to finish without putting a foot down wins.

materials.item: a path about 2 metres long, with a chappal at each end
a phone stopwatch, or a grown-up counting claps

schedule.what: Walk 2 metres as slowly as you can without ever stopping, and count the claps.

activities.record: Write your slowest number of claps. Draw how you moved your feet.

setup.art: A girl lifting one foot very slowly between two chappals, with her arms out for balance.
setup.caption: 1. Walk to the far chappal as slowly as you can.

setup.art: A grandfather counting claps and watching that the girl's feet never stop moving.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up counts claps and checks you never stop.

flow.do: Explain the rules: the slowest walker wins, but feet must keep moving all the time.
flow.say: This race is upside down. The slowest one wins. But you must never stand still. If you stop, you are out.
flow.kid: The slowest one wins. But you must never stop.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks the 2 metres as slowly as they can, while you count claps. 2. Try twice. 3. Swap, and you try too.
flow.say: Go! Slower, slower. Keep moving. How many claps did that take?
flow.kid: Move very slowly. Keep moving. Count the claps.
flow.parent: A slow race shows that speed works both ways. More claps for the same distance means slower.

flow.do: Compare the clap counts.
flow.say: Who took the most claps? So who was slowest? How did you keep so slow?
flow.kid: Who took the most claps? Who was slowest?

ask.q: How did you move so slowly?
good: I took tiny steps.
I lifted my feet very slowly.
I did both.

games.title: Who Won the Race?
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or 1 child with a grown-up
games.context: This is a card game about judging races. Each card tells of a race. Players say who was faster, or whether the race was fair, and then turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 16 race cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: Kavya walks to the door in 6 claps. Farhan walks to the same door in 9 claps. Who is faster?
items.b: Kavya. Same distance, and she took fewer claps.

items.f: Two ants walk for 10 claps. Ant A goes 2 tiles. Ant B goes 3 tiles. Who is faster?
items.b: Ant B. Same time, and she went further.

items.f: Meenakshi starts 3 steps ahead of her brother. She wins. Was it a fair race?
items.b: No. A fair race has the same start line for everyone.

items.f: Lakshmi runs before anyone says 'Go!'. She wins. Was it a fair race?
items.b: No. Everyone must start at the same 'Go!'.

items.f: Riya takes tiny quick steps. Sana takes ordinary steps. Who usually crosses the room first?
items.b: Sana. Tiny steps are quick but short, so they cover less ground each clap.

items.f: A snail and a tortoise race to a leaf 1 metre away. The tortoise gets there first. Who is slower?
items.b: The snail. Same distance, and the snail took longer.

items.f: Bisakha cycles for 1 minute and goes 200 metres. Her friend walks for 1 minute and goes 60 metres. Who is faster?
items.b: Bisakha. Same time, and she went further.

items.f: A slow walker starts ahead. In a very short race, who will probably win?
items.b: The slow walker. The race ends before the fast walker can catch up.

items.f: A slow walker starts ahead. In a very long race, who will probably win?
items.b: The fast walker. There is time to catch up and pass.

items.f: Two boats row for the same time. The green boat goes further. Which boat is faster?
items.b: The green boat. Same time, further distance.

items.f: Gurpreet claps fast for one racer and slowly for the other. Is the race fair?
items.b: No. The claps are the clock, so they must stay steady for everyone.

items.f: Nandini runs 50 metres in 12 seconds. Ishita runs 50 metres in 15 seconds. Who wins?
items.b: Nandini. Same distance, and she took less time.

items.f: A mosquito's wings beat hundreds of times a second. Can you run faster than a mosquito flies?
items.b: Yes. Each wing beat moves her only a tiny way, so she flies slowly.

items.f: Thenmozhi and Arjun race to the gate. They start together and arrive together. Who is faster?
items.b: Neither. Same distance and same time means the same speed.

items.f: A crow flies to a tree in 3 claps. A pigeon flies to the same tree in 4 claps. Who is faster?
items.b: The crow. Same distance, fewer claps.

items.f: A train and a car both travel for 1 hour. The train goes further. Which was faster?
items.b: The train. Same time, further distance.

rules: Cut out the cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
Take turns. The grown-up reads the top card aloud.
The player says the answer and why: same distance, or same time, or fair or not fair.
Turn the card over. If the player was right and gave the reason, they keep the card.
If not, the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is gone, the player with the most cards wins.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards cut from paper, stacked in a pile on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and stack them.

setup.art: A mother reading a card aloud to a girl, who points to a drawing of two ants on tiles.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, answer, then turn it over.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and read the rules together.
flow.say: Each card is a race. You say who was faster, and why. Was it the same distance, or the same time?
flow.kid: Each card is a race. Say who was faster, and why.

flow.do: Play through the pile. After each answer, ask: was the distance the same, or the time?
flow.say: Was it the same distance or the same time? So who was faster?
flow.kid: Same distance or same time? Who was faster?
flow.parent: The reason matters more than the name. Praise answers that say 'same distance, fewer claps' or 'same time, further'.

flow.do: Count the cards and talk about the hardest one.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why?

check.q: Thenmozhi and Arjun start together and reach the gate together. Who is faster?
options: Neither, they have the same speed
check.why: They went the same distance in the same time, so they have the same speed.

games.title: The Snake Boat Race board game
games.context: This is a board game about a boat race on a lake in Kerala. Players answer speed questions to row their boats from the jetty to the finish line.

printables.title: A race board with squares from the jetty to the finish line
items: Square 0: the start, at the boat jetty
Square 3: the crowd cheers, move on 1 more square
Square 5: oars out of time, miss a turn
Square 8: everyone sings the boat song, every boat moves on 1 square
Square 12: a long strong pull, move on 2 squares
Square 14: short splashy strokes, go back 1 square
Square 17: the crowd cheers, move on 1 more square

printables.title: 12 question cards, with the answer on the back

items.f: What is speed?
items.b: How far something goes in a stretch of time.

items.f: Two runners race the same distance. How do you know who is faster?
items.b: The one who takes less time, and finishes first.

items.f: Two runners run for the same time. How do you know who is faster?
items.b: The one who goes further.

items.f: Name one thing a fair race needs.
items.b: The same start line, the same finish line, or the same 'Go!' for everyone.

items.f: Name an animal faster than you.
items.b: For example a dog, a crow or a cheetah.

items.f: Name something slower than you.
items.b: For example a snail, an ant or a tortoise.

items.f: Why do tiny quick steps lose to an ordinary walk?
items.b: Each tiny step goes only a short way.

items.f: What is a head start?
items.b: Starting ahead of the others, closer to the finish.

items.f: Which wins a long race: a slow walker with a head start, or a fast walker?
items.b: Usually the fast walker, who has time to catch up and pass.

items.f: What is the fastest thing there is?
items.b: Light.

items.f: Why do rowers in a boat pull at the same moment?
items.b: So their pulls add up and push the boat forward together.

items.f: Say 'faster' or 'slower': a bullock cart compared with a bus.
items.b: Slower.

rules: Each player puts a boat on square 0.
Take turns. Another player reads you the top question card.
If you answer right, row on 3 squares. If not, row on 1 square.
If you land on a square with words, do what it says.
Put the card at the bottom of the pile.
The first boat to reach square 20 wins the race.

setup.art: A long paper board drawn as a lake, with squares numbered 0 to 20 and four paper boat tokens on square 0.
setup.caption: 1. Put the boats on the jetty, square 0.

setup.art: A boy reading a question card while a girl moves her green boat 3 squares along the board.
setup.caption: 2. Answer a card, then row on 3 squares or 1.

flow.do: Draw the board, cut out the boats and the cards, and read the rules.
flow.say: This is a boat race in Kerala. Answer right and your boat rows 3 squares. Answer wrong and it rows only 1.
flow.kid: Answer right and row 3 squares. Wrong, and row 1.

flow.do: Play until one boat reaches square 20.
flow.say: You landed on 'short splashy strokes'. Why do those make a boat go back?
flow.kid: Why do short splashy strokes make the boat slower?
flow.parent: When a player lands on square 12 or 14, ask why long pulls help and splashy strokes do not.

flow.do: Talk about who won and why.
flow.say: Who won? Did the winner answer more cards right? So was that boat faster?
flow.kid: Who won? Why was that boat faster?

projects.title: The Sprout Race: whose root grows fastest?
projects.context: In this project you race three kinds of seeds: moong, chana and methi. Each day you measure their roots. Speed is not only for runners. Growing has a speed too.

materials.item: a small handful each of whole moong, whole chana and methi seeds
3 small bowls or katoris, for soaking
a plate with a wet cotton cloth or a few layers of wet tissue
a ruler with centimetres
paper and a pencil for a growth table

schedule.what: Soak 5 seeds of each kind in water overnight, in separate bowls.
Lay the seeds on the wet cloth in three rows. Guess which root will grow longest. Measure any roots.
Measure the longest root in each row. Keep the cloth wet.
Measure again. Which seed is winning?
Measure one last time. Work out how much each root grew from day 4 to day 5.

projects.record: A growth table with the longest root of each seed for each day, and a drawing of the three rows on day 5.

setup.art: Three small steel katoris with moong, chana and methi soaking in water.
setup.caption: 1. Soak each kind of seed overnight.

setup.art: A plate with a wet cotton cloth and three rows of seeds, with small white roots showing.
setup.caption: 2. Lay three rows on the wet cloth.

setup.art: A child's hand holding a ruler beside a moong sprout's white root.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the longest root in each row each day.

flow.do: Day 1: put 5 seeds of each kind in its own bowl and cover them with water.
flow.say: These seeds will race. Not on legs, but by growing. Tomorrow we lay them out.
flow.kid: Soak the seeds tonight. Tomorrow the race begins.

flow.do: Day 2: lay the seeds on the wet cloth in three rows. Ask your child to guess the winner.
flow.say: Which seed's root will grow longest by day 5? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which root will grow longest? Why?
flow.parent: Keep the plate out of strong sun and keep the cloth damp. Moong usually sprouts first. If a seed does not sprout, leave that seed out of the race.

flow.do: Days 3 to 5: measure the longest root in each row with the ruler and write it in the table.
flow.say: How long is the moong root today? How much did it grow since yesterday?
flow.kid: Measure each root. Write the number in the table.
flow.parent: Each seed's root grows towards the wet cloth and away from the light. The seeds sense the water and the pull of the Earth, and grow their roots where they need to.

flow.do: Day 5: compare the growth from day 4 to day 5 for each seed.
flow.say: Which root grew the most in one day? That seed's root was growing fastest.
flow.kid: Which root grew most in one day? That one was fastest.

check.q: In one day, the moong root grew 2 centimetres and the chana root grew 1 centimetre. Which was growing faster?
check.why: In the same time, one day, the moong root grew further. So it was growing faster.

challenges.title: The Slow Lane: make a marble take as long as possible
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A marble rolls down a tilted tray very fast. Your job is to build a path that makes it take as many claps as you can to reach the bottom.
challenges.problem: Can you build a path on a tilted tray that makes a marble take as long as possible to reach the bottom, without ever stopping?
constraints: The tray stays tilted on one book the whole time.
You let the marble go from the top. You may not touch it after that.
The marble must reach the bottom by itself. If it gets stuck, that try does not count.
materials: a tray or a big steel plate with a rim
one book, to tilt the tray
a marble, or a dry round chana
pencils, straws, strips of card and small rolls of atta dough, to make walls
general: Lay pencils across the tray at a slant, with a lump of dough at each end to hold them, so the marble rolls from side to side in a zigzag.
Make the path longer, so the marble has further to go.
Put a gentle bump of dough in the way, so the marble slows down before it rolls over.
creative: Make a spiral of dough walls, so the marble rolls round and round before it reaches the bottom.
Lay a strip of cloth on part of the path, so the marble rolls more slowly there.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own slow lane. Count the claps. Then change one wall at a time, and see if the marble takes even longer.

setup.art: A steel tray tilted on one book, with a marble rolling straight down it.
setup.caption: 1. First, let the marble roll straight down. Count the claps.

setup.art: The same tray with pencils laid across it at a slant, making a zigzag path.
setup.caption: 2. Build walls to make a zigzag path.

setup.art: A child counting claps as a marble zigzags slowly down the tray.
setup.caption: 3. Let go, and count the claps again.

flow.do: Tilt the tray on one book. Let the marble roll straight down while you clap.
flow.say: Straight down, that took only about one clap. Can you make it take five?
flow.kid: Straight down is fast. Can you make it slow?

flow.do: Your child builds walls and tests them. Count the claps each time.
flow.say: How many claps this time? Which wall made the biggest difference?
flow.kid: Build walls. Let go. Count the claps.
flow.parent: A zigzag makes the path longer, so the same marble takes more time. The marble did not change. The distance did.

flow.do: Show the best path and talk about why it was slow.
flow.say: Why did your path take so many claps? Was the marble slower, or did it go further, or both?
flow.kid: Why did your path take so long?

ask.q: Why did the zigzag take more claps?
good: The path was longer.
The marble had to go further.
The walls slowed it down at each turn.

items.p: Draw a line from each racer to the word that fits: faster or slower than you running.
items.why: A cheetah and a train go further than you in the same time. A snail and a tortoise go a shorter way.
items.art: Four small pictures on the left: a cheetah, a snail, a train and a tortoise, and the words faster and slower on the right.

items.p: In the Step Race, you walked the same path three ways. How did you know which way was fastest?
opts: It made my feet move fastest
items.why: The distance was the same each time. So the way that took the least time, the fewest claps, was the fastest.

items.p: Draw two footprint trails across the same room: one with tiny steps and one with your ordinary steps.
items.a: Two trails of the same length. The tiny-step trail has many footprints close together. The ordinary trail has fewer footprints, further apart.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that tiny steps need many more footprints to cover the same distance.
items.art: An empty box with a start line on the left and a finish line on the right.

items.p: True or false: in a fair race, everyone starts from the same line.
items.why: True. If someone starts closer to the finish, the race is not fair.

items.p: Remember the Freeze Race, where you moved for 4 claps. Sort these: FAIR or NOT FAIR.
items: Everyone starts at the same chappal
items.why: A fair race keeps the time or the distance the same for everyone. Extra claps or a closer start are not fair.

items.p: Speed is how ___ something goes in a stretch of time.
items.why: Speed tells you how far a thing goes in a stretch of time.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the Step Race, why did tiny steps take more claps than your ordinary walk?
items.a: Each tiny step went only a little way, so I needed many more steps to get there.
items.why: A strong answer says the steps were short, not only that they were tiny. Short steps add up to less ground in each clap.

items.p: In the Step Race, Riya took 10 claps with tiny steps and 4 claps with her ordinary walk. How many more claps did the tiny steps take?
Label the picture of a race: start line, finish line, racer, the person saying 'Go!'.
a: start line: where the racers stand at the beginning
finish line: where the race ends
racer: a child walking along the path
the person saying 'Go!': the grown-up at the side
items.why: Knowing each part helps you check a race is fair. A strong answer puts each label on the right part.
items.art: A hallway with a chappal at each end, a child walking, and a woman at the side with her hand up, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A cheetah, a crow flying, a snail, a train.
items.why: The snail is slower than you. The other three are faster than you.

items.p: Three friends watched the Step Race, where a girl walked the same path with tiny steps, giant steps and her ordinary walk.

views.says: Tiny steps should win, because her feet moved the fastest.
Her ordinary walk won, because each step went a good way and came quickly too.
Giant steps should win, because she needed the fewest steps.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own Step Race. Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer usually agrees with Revathi, using the clap counts from the test. Kavya is right that tiny steps come fastest, but each one is short. Farhan is right that giant steps are fewest, but each one is slow.
items.why: Speed depends on both how far each step goes and how often a step comes. Each friend saw one half of that.

items.p: Sana and her grandfather race to the door. Sana takes 4 claps. Her grandfather takes 4 claps too. What can you say?
items.why: Same distance and same time means the same speed.

items.p: In the Head-Start Race, the slow grown-up won the short race but lost the long one. Their speeds never changed. Why did the winner change?
items.a: The faster walker was catching up all the time. In the short race the finish came before they caught up. In the long race there was time to catch up and pass.
items.why: A strong answer says the faster walker gains every clap, and that the length of the race decides whether there is time to pass.

items.p: Put these in order from slowest to fastest.
items: a cycle on an open road
a: a cycle on an open road
items.why: A snail crawls slower than you walk. A cycle goes faster than walking. An aeroplane is the fastest of these.

items.p: True or false: the hare and tortoise story shows that slow racers always win.
items.why: False. The tortoise wins only because the hare stops to sleep. If the hare kept running, the hare would win.

items.p: Draw the Head-Start Race path. Show both start lines, the near finish, the far finish and the place where you caught up.
items.a: A line with the child's start at the back, the grown-up's start ahead, the near finish just past the grown-up's start, the catch-up mark a little further, and the far finish beyond it.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the catch-up mark between the near finish and the far finish. That shows why the short race and the long race had different winners.
items.art: A long empty box for a hallway, seen from above.

items.p: Match each race to the fair way to judge it.
pairs: Everyone swims one length of the pool
items.why: When the distance is the same, the shortest time wins. When the time is the same, the longest distance wins.

items.p: Hema walked 10 tiles in 5 claps. She walked the same number of tiles in each clap. How many tiles did she walk in each clap?
items.why: 10 shared into 5 equal claps is 2 each. Check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10.

items.p: In the Freeze Race, all three ways had the same 4 claps. Why does that make it a fair way to compare them?
items.a: Because only the way of moving changed. The time was the same, so the one that went furthest really was the fastest.
items.why: A strong answer says the time was kept the same, so the distance shows the speed.

items.p: Which race is the odd one out, because it is not fair?
opts: Both start at the same chappal
Both run to the same door
items.why: Starting halfway gives one racer a head start, so the race is not fair. The others keep the race fair.

items.p: Two friends are arguing about whether a slow racer can ever win.

views.says: The faster racer always wins. That is what faster means.
A slower racer can win if they start ahead and the race is short.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the Head-Start Race as your evidence. Then say when the other friend would be right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Thenmozhi, because the slow grown-up won the short race with a head start. Bisakha is right in a fair race with the same start line: then the faster racer always wins.
items.why: In a fair race, the faster racer wins. With a head start, the length of the race decides.

items.p: A mosquito beats her wings hundreds of times each second. Yet you can run away from her. Explain why, using what you found in the Step Race.
items.a: Each wing beat moves the mosquito only a tiny way, just as each tiny step moved me only a foot's length. Many quick movements can still add up to a slow speed.
items.why: A strong answer links the quick, short wing beats to the quick, short steps in the Step Race.

items.p: Arjun rolls a toy car slowly down the aisle of a bus that is speeding along the road. Compared with the bus, the car is slow. Compared with the road, is the car slow or fast?
opts: Fast, because the bus carries it along
items.why: Compared with the bus, the car is slow. Compared with the road, it moves with the bus, so it is fast. Speed is always compared with something.

items.p: Draw a race that is NOT fair. Then draw a cross on what makes it unfair, and write how to fix it.
items.a: For example, one runner starting halfway, crossed out, with the words 'start at the same line'.
items.why: A strong answer shows one clear unfair thing and a fix that makes the start, the finish or the 'Go!' the same for everyone.

items.p: Sort these ways of judging a race: SAME DISTANCE or SAME TIME.
items: Who swims one length in fewest seconds?
Who walks most tiles in 1 minute?
items.why: Reaching a place first or in fewest seconds keeps the distance the same. Going furthest in a set time keeps the time the same.

items.p: Grandma has a head start of 6 tiles. Each clap, Grandma walks 1 tile and Meena walks 3 tiles. After how many claps does Meena catch up?
items.why: After 1 clap: Grandma 7, Meena 3. After 2: Grandma 8, Meena 6. After 3: Grandma 9, Meena 9. They are level after 3 claps.

items.p: In the Sprout Race, the moong root grew 2 centimetres in one day. Is a growing root moving? Is it fast or slow? Give a reason.
items.a: Yes, the root tip moves as it grows. You can see it is slow: it took a whole day to grow 2 centimetres. A snail goes much further in a day.
items.why: A strong answer says growing is moving, and that fast or slow depends on what you compare it with.

items.p: True or false: when you sit still on the floor, you are moving compared with the Sun.
items.why: True. You are still compared with the room. But the Earth is carrying you round the Sun, very fast.

items.p: Label the boat race picture: long pull, short splashy stroke, the singer, the faster boat.

short splashy stroke: an oar throwing up spray in the blue boat
the singer: the person standing in the green boat who sings
the faster boat: the green boat, ahead
items.why: A strong answer marks the green boat as faster, because each long pull moves it further.

opts: How far something goes in a stretch of time
quiz.why: Speed tells you how far a thing goes in a stretch of time. Weight and size are different things.

quiz.p: Meera and Zoya walk to the same door. Meera takes 5 claps and Zoya takes 8 claps. Who is faster?
quiz.why: The distance is the same, and Meera took fewer claps. Picking Zoya means counting more claps as more speed. More claps means more time, so slower.

quiz.p: Two children ride cycles for 1 minute. Chitra goes 150 metres. Hema goes 100 metres. Who is faster?
quiz.why: The time is the same, and Chitra went further. So she is faster.

opts: Everyone starts at one line and goes at the same 'Go!'
The youngest starts closer to the finish
Each runner starts when they feel ready
quiz.why: A fair race has the same start, the same finish and the same signal for everyone. A head start is kind, but it is not a fair test of speed.

quiz.p: Kavya crossed the room with tiny quick steps and then with her ordinary walk. Which usually takes fewer claps?
quiz.why: Each tiny step covers only a foot's length, so tiny steps take more claps. Picking tiny steps means judging speed by how busy the feet look.

quiz.p: How fast you walk depends on what?
opts: How long your steps are and how often you take them
Only how fast your feet move
Only how long your legs are
quiz.why: Speed needs both: the length of each step and how many steps you take in a clap.

quiz.p: A slow walker starts well ahead of a fast walker. Which race will the slow walker most likely win?
quiz.why: The fast walker gains a little every clap. In a short race, the finish comes before the fast walker catches up.

quiz.p: In the hare and tortoise story, why does the tortoise win?
quiz.why: A hare runs much faster than a tortoise walks. The tortoise wins only because the hare stops for a long time.

quiz.p: Why should claps be steady when you use them to time a race?
opts: So every racer is timed the same way
quiz.why: The claps are the clock. If they speed up or slow down, the race is not fair.

quiz.p: Before a test, what should you do first?
opts: Guess what will happen and say why
quiz.why: A guess with a reason lets the test show you whether your idea was right.

quiz.p: A mosquito beats her wings very fast. Why can you still run away from her?
opts: Each wing beat moves her only a tiny way
quiz.why: Many quick, tiny movements can add up to a slow speed, like tiny quick steps.

quiz.p: What is the fastest thing there is?
quiz.why: Light travels about 3 lakh kilometres every second. Nothing has been found that goes faster.

applications: Races at school sports days and at the Olympics are judged by time over the same distance.
Traffic police use speed limits and speed cameras to keep roads safe.
Train timetables are worked out from how far the train goes and how fast it runs.
Coaches help runners go faster by working on both stride length and how quickly they step.
Weather scientists measure wind speed to warn of cyclones on the coasts of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
Doctors and nurses count how fast a heart beats, in beats each minute.

open_questions.q: What is the fastest any animal could ever run?
open_questions.why_open: A cheetah can reach more than 90 kilometres an hour for a short burst. Scientists still argue about what sets the limit for any land animal: muscles, bones, heat or breathing.

open_questions.q: Why does the universe have a speed limit, the speed of light?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists have tested that nothing goes faster than light, many times. Nobody knows why the limit has the value it has.

open_questions.q: How does an ant decide how fast to walk?
open_questions.why_open: Ants walk faster when it is warm. How an ant senses her surroundings and sets her speed is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How fast do our thoughts go?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure how fast signals travel along nerves. But a thought uses many parts of the body at once, and nobody can yet say how long one thought takes.

maths.problem: In the Step Race, Riya's tiny steps took 8 claps and her ordinary walk took 3 claps. How many more claps did the tiny steps take?
maths.explain: Start at 3 and count on to 8: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is 5 counts. So the tiny steps took 5 more claps. More claps for the same distance means slower.
maths.context: This is about the Step Race, where you walked the same path with tiny steps, giant steps and your ordinary walk.
maths.why_maths: Taking one number from the other tells you how much slower one way was, not just that it was slower.

maths.problem: In the Step Race, Farhan's giant steps took 4 claps, 9 claps and 4 claps. Which try looks like a fluke, and how many claps did giant steps really take?
maths.answer: The try with 9 claps looks like a fluke. Giant steps really took about 4 claps.
maths.explain: Two tries gave 4 claps and one gave 9. The 9 is far from the others. Maybe Farhan wobbled or the clapping slipped. So we trust the 4, and try once more to check.
maths.context: This is about the Step Race, where each way of walking was tried three times.
maths.why_maths: Comparing three tries shows which one is odd, so one fluke does not fool you.

maths.problem: Lakshmi walked 12 tiles in 4 claps. She walked the same number of tiles in each clap. How many tiles did she walk in each clap?
maths.explain: 12 tiles shared into 4 equal claps is 3 tiles in each clap. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Tiles in each clap is a way to say her speed.
maths.context: This is about counting tiles on the floor as you walk, the way you counted claps in the Step Race.
maths.why_maths: Sharing the distance into equal parts tells you how far she goes in one clap, which is her speed.

maths.problem: Amma has a head start of 8 tiles. Each clap, Amma walks 1 tile and Meena walks 3 tiles. After how many claps does Meena catch up?
maths.explain: Make a table. After 1 clap: Amma 9, Meena 3. After 2: Amma 10, Meena 6. After 3: Amma 11, Meena 9. After 4: Amma 12, Meena 12. Each clap Meena gains 2 tiles, and 8 tiles take 4 claps to make up.
maths.context: This is about the Head-Start Race, where a slow walker began ahead of a faster walker.
maths.why_maths: A table of claps shows the gap shrinking by the same amount each time, so you can predict where the catch-up will be.

maths.problem: In the Sprout Race, the moong root was 1 centimetre long on day 2, 3 centimetres on day 3 and 5 centimetres on day 4. If it keeps growing the same way, how long will it be on day 5?
maths.explain: Each day the root grew 2 more centimetres: 1, 3, 5. The next number is 5 and 2 more, which is 7. A real root may slow down or speed up, so measure to check.
maths.context: This is about the Sprout Race, where you measured the roots of moong, chana and methi each day.
maths.why_maths: Spotting how much the root grows each day lets you guess its speed of growing before you measure.

roots.context: We have raced across the room, counted claps and given a slow walker a head start. Now we ask what speed tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your tiny steps came very fast, yet they lost to your ordinary walk. Each tiny step covered only a foot's length. How fast you go depends on how far each step reaches and how often you take one. So feet that look busy can still be slow.
deep_truth.habit: We judge speed by how busy something looks: whirring legs, flapping wings, splashing oars. But busy movement is only half of speed. How far each movement carries you is the other half.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Step Race, tiny quick steps took the most steps and usually the most claps. The ordinary walk took fewer steps and fewer claps. In the story, the boat with the fastest oars lost to the boat with long pulls.

three.who_am_i: You are a walker who chooses your own speed. You change it by changing how long your steps are and how quickly you take them.
three.what_is_life: Everything is conscious, and every living being moves at their own speed. A sprout grows slowly and a crow flies fast. Each one senses when to hurry and when to rest.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything in the world is moving compared with something else. Even the floor under you is carried round the Sun by the Earth.

roots.thread: Speed joins two things: how far, and how long. A sprout, an ant, a boat and you all move through the same space and the same time. Each moves at their own speed, by their own mix of step length and pace.

teachings.source: Zeno of Elea, as told by Aristotle in his Physics, Book 6, chapter 9
teachings.teaching: Zeno, a Greek thinker, told a puzzle. Swift Achilles races a tortoise who has a head start. When Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, the tortoise has moved a little further on. Zeno asked how Achilles could ever catch up.
teachings.link: In the Head-Start Race, you did catch up, and you marked the exact place. Zeno's puzzle is old, but you showed that a faster racer does pass.

teachings.source: Nagarjuna, Mulamadhyamakakarika (Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way), chapter 2
teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna, an Indian Buddhist thinker, asked where going happens. It is not on the path already walked, and not on the path still to walk. He showed that going, the goer and the path depend on each other.
teachings.link: A speed also needs more than the walker. It needs a path, a distance and a time. Take away any one, and there is no speed to measure.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching, a Chinese book of wisdom, says that a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
teachings.link: In the Step Race, every journey across the room was made of single steps. How long each step was, and how often it came, decided how soon you arrived.

science.text: Every speed is measured compared with something else, usually the ground. The Earth carries all of us round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second.
Nothing has been found that travels faster than light in empty space. Why the universe has this speed limit is still unknown.

other_view.view: Speed is only a number people work out, a distance divided by a time. It describes how something moves, and says nothing about any choice or awareness in the ant, the sprout or the boat.

practice.title: Still and Carried
practice.say: Sit very still on the floor and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly. Your body is still compared with the room. Now remember that the Earth is carrying you round the Sun. It is carrying the floor, the walls and everyone you know. Feel how still you are. Then open your eyes slowly.
practice.kid: Sit very still. Close your eyes. Breathe in and out slowly. You are still in the room. But the Earth is carrying you round the Sun. Feel how still you are. Open your eyes slowly.

how_we_found_out.context: Does light take time to travel, or does it arrive at once? This card tells how people found out.
how_we_found_out.who: Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in Cairo; René Descartes, a French thinker; and Ole Rømer, a Danish astronomer working at the Paris Observatory
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Light does not travel at all. It arrives everywhere at the same instant.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, many people thought light needs no time to travel. Switch on a lamp, and the whole room is lit at once. About 1,000 years ago, Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in Cairo, argued that light must move, and so must take some time. But he could not measure it. Hundreds of years later, René Descartes, a French thinker, still taught that light arrives in an instant. In 1676, Ole Rømer, a Danish astronomer in Paris, was timing Io, one of Jupiter's moons. Io goes behind Jupiter again and again, like clockwork. But Rømer saw that Io seemed to come out late when the Earth was far from Jupiter, and early when it was near. He worked out why. When the Earth is further away, the light from Io has further to travel, so it reaches us later. So light does take time. Today we know that sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a city flat. The Step Race needs a 4 metre path, which most flats have along a hall or across the main room. Children walk, never run, barefoot on tiles. In the Head-Start Race, the grown-up takes one heel-to-toe step per clap, which keeps the slow speed the same every time: with a head start of 4 big steps, the grown-up wins the race to 2 foot-lengths past their start, and the child catches up well before the cushion 3 big steps further on. The Freeze Race and the Slow Race need only a short stretch of floor. Moong, chana and methi are kitchen staples, and moong sprouts within a day or two on wet cloth.
